title: Grade XI Physics – Unit 3 Translatory Motion: Summative MCQ Practice
sourceDocument: NBF Grade XI Physics Unit 3 (textbook pp. 33–52) and FBISE Physics HSSC-I 50% model paper / assessment framework
sourceSection: 28 straight MCQs, 12 original scenario MCQs in 3 four-question situations; 5 adapted from Unit 3 textbook exercise; 35 original SLO-based practice items
limitations: Educational practice only. Provisional original questions, answers and explanations subject to final teacher/scientific review; not an official FBISE model paper, secure assessment or complete 80-item examination. Only summative theory SLOs P-11-B-04/05/06/12/13 included. Formative B-03 and B-11 intentionally excluded.

structure.modeledAfter: FBISE HSSC-I Section A (56 straight + 24 scenario in full 80-MCQ pattern), scaled to 40-question unit-only practice

questions.stem: A ball is projected vertically upward with initial velocity 19.6 m/s. Taking upward as positive, its velocity after 1 s is:
questions.explanation: v = u − gt = 19.6 − 9.8(1) = +9.8 m/s, still upward.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: A particle has initial velocity −4 m/s and acceleration +2 m/s² along a straight line. Its velocity after 3 s is:
questions.explanation: v = −4 + (2)(3) = +2 m/s; a positive sign indicates motion in the chosen positive direction.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: In ideal projectile motion, the velocity and acceleration vectors are perpendicular at:
questions.explanation: At the highest point, vertical velocity is zero and velocity is horizontal; acceleration remains vertically downward.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Which description best represents projectile motion after launch, in the absence of air resistance?

options.text: An object moving entirely independently of gravity
Only an object projected exactly vertically upward
An object moving under gravity after being projected into the air
Only horizontal motion without any gravitational force

questions.explanation: After launch, gravity acts on the projectile; the horizontal and vertical components of motion evolve independently.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: At which location is the magnitude of an ideal projectile's vertical velocity component the smallest?

options.text: At landing at the launch height
At one-quarter of the flight time

questions.explanation: At the top, vᵧ = 0, the minimum possible magnitude.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: After an ideal projectile has been released, the only force acting on it (neglecting air resistance) is:

options.text: A magnetic force due to its motion

questions.explanation: Once the launching contact ends, the ideal projectile experiences its gravitational force (weight) only.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: For a fixed launch speed onto level ground, and no air resistance, the maximum projectile range is obtained at:
questions.explanation: R = (u²/g)sin(2θ), maximized when sin(2θ)=1, so θ = 45°.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s and 30° above level ground. With g = 9.8 m/s² and no air resistance, its flight time is approximately:
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 60° above horizontal. Its horizontal velocity at the highest point is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal velocity remains constant: uₓ = u cos60° = 10 m/s.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: During forward flight through still air, the horizontal velocity component of a projectile experiencing air resistance generally:

options.text: Reverses direction at the highest point

questions.explanation: Air drag acts opposite the forward motion; its horizontal component reduces horizontal speed.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: While a projectile is ascending, the vertical component of air resistance normally acts:

options.text: In the same direction as its velocity

questions.explanation: Drag opposes velocity; during ascent its vertical component acts downward, along with gravity.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Compared with an otherwise identical ideal launch, air resistance generally makes the projectile's horizontal range:
questions.explanation: Air drag reduces the projectile's forward motion; for otherwise identical conditions, its range is generally reduced.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Two ideal projectiles at complementary launch angles have equal range at fixed speed and equal heights. With air resistance this equality:
questions.explanation: R(θ)=R(90°−θ) follows from the ideal no-drag range formula; drag generally destroys the symmetry.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: In an ideal isolated elastic collision, which two total physical quantities are conserved?

options.text: Momentum and speed of each body
Kinetic energy and the velocity of each body
Momentum and the direction of motion of each body

questions.explanation: Elastic collisions conserve total momentum and total kinetic energy of the isolated system.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Two identical masses collide elastically head-on. The second is initially at rest. Their velocities after collision:
questions.explanation: For equal masses in a 1-D elastic collision, the moving body stops and the initially stationary target takes its velocity.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: In an ideal head-on elastic collision, if the relative speed of approach is 6 m/s, the relative speed of separation is:
questions.explanation: Relative speed of separation equals relative speed of approach for an ideal elastic collision.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: If total kinetic energy before an isolated elastic collision is 80 J, the total kinetic energy afterward is:
questions.explanation: Total kinetic energy is conserved in an isolated elastic collision, so it remains 80 J.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Which statement is correct for an isolated system during an inelastic collision?

options.text: Both momentum and kinetic energy must always increase
Total momentum is destroyed when deformation occurs
Each object's momentum remains individually unchanged
Total momentum is conserved even though total kinetic energy may decrease

questions.explanation: The isolated system conserves total momentum, but some kinetic energy can transform into heat, sound or deformation.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: In an inelastic collision, part of the initial kinetic energy may be transferred into:

options.text: An increase in the system's external impulse

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy can change form in an inelastic collision; this does not violate overall energy conservation.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Two objects stick together after a head-on collision. Their final velocities must:

options.text: Be equal in magnitude but opposite in direction

questions.explanation: Sticking is the perfectly inelastic special case: both objects move together with one common final velocity.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: A 4 kg body moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg body and they stick together. Their final shared velocity is:
questions.explanation: Momentum before = (4)(3)+(2)(0)=12 kg·m/s; shared v = 12/(4+2)=2 m/s.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Which conclusion best explains a decrease in total kinetic energy after an isolated collision?

options.text: Some kinetic energy has changed form, although total momentum is conserved
Total momentum must decrease by the same percentage
The law of conservation of energy has been violated
The mass of both objects must become zero

questions.explanation: Some mechanical kinetic energy converts into other forms; total momentum remains conserved in an isolated interaction.
